question: What did you say in your first address at the Parliament of Religions in Chicago?

result.text: I spoke at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago, where I expressed my gratitude for the warm and cordial welcome given to me and my fellow delegates.[1] I thanked the audience in the name of the most ancient order of monks in the world, the mother of religions, and millions of Hindu people of all classes and sects.[1] I emphasized the importance of representing Hinduism in a manner that was clear, correct, and authoritative, which left a remarkable impression at the Parliament of Religions itself.[2] I called attention to the characteristic Hindu doctrine of the Harmony and Brotherhood of Religions, highlighting the unity of all faiths in their pursuit of Truth.[2] I stated that no longer could it be insisted that Truth and Holiness were the exclusive possessions of any particular locality or system of doctrine.[2] I used the language of the Bhagavad-Gitâ to illustrate the sweet harmony in the heart of all religions, all leading to the same goal.[2]

question: How did your view of Buddhism relate to Hinduism in your Chicago addresses?

result.text: As I stated in my lecture at the Parliament of Religions, I am not a Buddhist, as you have heard, and yet I am.[1] I explained that the relation between Hinduism and modern Buddhism is nearly the same as between Judaism and Christianity.[1] I emphasized that Shâkya Muni came not to destroy, but to fulfil and not to destroy the teachings of the Hindu religion.[1] I noted that the real difference between modern Buddhism and the teachings of Lord Buddha lies in the fact that his own followers did not realise the import of his teachings.[1] I pointed out that the Jews rejected Jesus Christ, while the Hindus have accepted Shâkya Muni as God and worship him.[1] I argued that the Buddhist command could only be carried out through monasticism, while Hinduism might be fulfilled through any state of life.[2] I stated that the great point of contrast between Buddhism and Hinduism lies in the fact that Buddhism said, 'Realise all this as illusion', while Hinduism said, 'Realise that within the illusion is the Real.'[2]

question: What did you write to Alasinga about starting work in Madras?

result.text: I wrote to Alasinga from the U. S. a in 1894-08-31, urging him to organise a Society to take charge of the practical and pecuniary part of the work in Madras.[1] I told Alasinga that it would be a wonderful relief to me to get rid of horrid money affairs by having a Society handle them.[1] I encouraged Alasinga to work quickly and write to me, giving the society a non-sectarian name.[1] I asked Alasinga to get some of the big folks to be named as office-bearers of the Society, while he worked in the real sense.[1] I told Alasinga that if his duties were too severe, he could let G. G. do the business part, and I hoped to make him independent of his college work so that he could devote his whole soul to the work.[1] I wrote to Alasinga from London in 1896-11-20, mentioning that I intended to see a little of Ceylon and then go to Madras.[2]

question: What did you say about the condition of the masses in India?

result.text: I spoke about the condition of the masses in India, describing them as a conquered race and a nation of mendicants, with the lowest castes having lost their manliness and becoming like professional beggars.[1] I noted that the masses are so poor and ignorant about secular things that they are not violent, unlike the European masses, and that poverty here is not a crime.[2] I emphasized that the great national sin is the neglect of the masses, and that no amount of politics would be of any avail until they are well educated, well fed, and well cared for.[3] I described the masses as three hundred millions of souls crushed out of life by being downtrodden by their own people and foreign nations, patient in labour and suffering, and devoid of initiative like the slave.[4] I stated that the masses are practically our slaves, and that if we want to regenerate India, we must work for them.[3] I mentioned that the masses are very good because poverty here is not a crime, and that they are not violent, unlike in America and England where I was near being mobbed in America and England only on account of my dress.[2]

question: What was your position on the caste system?

result.text: I argued that the caste system is a social custom, not a religious institution, and that all our great preachers have tried to break it down.[1] I stated that caste is simply the outgrowth of the political institutions of India; it is a hereditary trade guild.[1] I noted that trade competition with Europe has broken caste more than any teaching.[1] I explained that the caste system has nothing to do with religion, and that a man's occupation is hereditary.[2] I acknowledged that the hereditary caste system of India is unable to overstep its own bounds, but that it is slowly conducing to the advancement of the people moving within the same circle.[3] I said that caste is a very good thing, and that it is the plan we want to follow, with the goal of making everybody a Brahmin.[4] I emphasized that caste is not a granted system of classes, but that each caste thought itself to be superior to all the others.[5] I described the caste system as having grown by the practice of the son always following the business of the father, and that it united the people by binding them to help their fellows in case of need.[6]

question: What did you say about the education of women in India?

result.text: I argued that our right of interference is limited entirely to giving education, and that women must be put in a position to solve their own problems in their own way.[1] I stated that our Indian women are as capable of solving their own problems as any in the world.[1] I noted that in modern times there is a greater impetus towards higher education on the European lines, and the trend of opinion is strong towards women getting this higher education.[2] I pointed out that our religion does not prevent a woman being educated at all, and that the girl should be educated in the spirit of our own religious ordinances.[2] I emphasized that the uplift of the women and the awakening of the masses must come first, and then only can any real good come about for the country, for India.[3] I stressed that female education must be spread with religion as its centre, and that all other training should be secondary to religion.[4] I observed that the whole work of educating women must be done in the style of our own country, with centres started for teaching women and Brahmacharinis of education and character taking up the task.[3]

question: How did you describe your Master, Shri Ramakrishna, in your lectures?

result.text: I described Shri Ramakrishna as a great soul whose influence has spread beyond India, and I owe all my spiritual teachings to him.[1] I spoke of Shri Ramakrishna as one who incarnated and experienced the unity underlying everything, having discovered it in Hinduism, Islam, and Christianity.[2] I recounted how my Master, Shri Ramakrishna, refused to use his mental power for his own healing, instead dedicating his mind entirely to God.[3] I emphasized that Shri Ramakrishna's teachings have become widely known and revered across India, with large gatherings celebrating his birthday anniversary.[4] I noted that Shri Ramakrishna's influence has grown significantly over time, with many people now recognizing and revering him.[4] I mentioned that Shri Ramakrishna's teachings have spread like wild fire, and today all India knows and reverences him.[4]

question: What did you tell the people of Madras when you returned from the West?

result.text: As I told the people of Madras upon my return from the West, I expressed my heartfelt welcome and gratitude for their support during my religious mission.[1] I conveyed my joy and pleasure at my safe return to India and congratulated them on the success of my efforts in Western lands.[2] I emphasized that the contradictions of the world's creeds are reconciled in the universal light of the Vedanta, and that unity in variety is nature's plan in the evolution of the universe.[2] I expressed my hope that under my auspices, a new era of peace, sympathy, and love would reign among men.[2] I also mentioned that the Western world had come to understand the inexhaustible store of spirituality India has even today.[2] I expressed my belief that the West would increasingly appreciate the sublime truths of Vedanta.[3] I reiterated my motto of 'Help, and not Fight', 'Assimilation, and not Destruction', 'Harmony and Peace, and not Dissension'.[3]

question: What did you say about idol worship when questioned in the West?

result.text: As I spoke at the Parliament of Religions, I explained that external worship, material worship, is the lowest stage of spiritual development, and that mental prayer is the next, with the highest being the realisation of the Lord.[1] I acknowledged that the same earnest man who kneels before an idol also says that the Sun, moon, stars, and fire cannot express the divine, and that he does not abuse any one's idol or call its worship sin.[1] I argued that all these various Pratikas and Pratimas lead to God, and that the worship of Buddha and of Christ constitutes a Pratika, a drawing near to the worship of God.[2] I stated that we may worship anything by seeing God in it, if we can forget the idol and see God there, but we must not project any image upon God.[2] I noted that the idea of a Personal God has obtained in almost every religion, except a very few, and that the Buddhists and the Jains, although they have no Personal God, worship the founders of their religions in precisely the same way as others worship a Personal God.[3] I observed that throughout the history of the world, man is trying to grasp the abstract through thought-forms or symbols, and that all the external manifestations of religion — bells, music, rituals, books, and images — come under that head.[3]

question: What did you write about the relationship between science and religion?

result.text: I wrote that science is nothing but the finding of unity, and as soon as science would reach perfect unity, it would stop from further progress, because it would reach the goal.[1] I explained that in all religions of the world, it is claimed that there is a unity within us, and being one with the Divinity, there cannot be any further progress in that sense.[2] I stated that the science of religion is based on the analysis of the human soul and has no creed, unlike other sciences.[3] I emphasized that experience is the only source of knowledge, and in the world, religion is the only science where there is no surety, because it is not taught as a science of experience.[4] I noted that the grand principle of religion has already been mapped out for us, and our work lies in filling it in, working it out, and applying it to every part of our lives.[5] I pointed out that the science of religion is similar to mathematics in every part of the world, as the mystics do not differ and their experience becomes law.[4] I argued that the science of religion is not limited by the external world, as the human mind is not homogeneous and requires different methods based on individual nature.[3] I warned that there is a superstition in the matter of science, and we should be cautious, analysing, testing, and proving everything before accepting it.[6]

question: What did you say about Christ in your lecture 'Christ, the Messenger'?

result.text: As I spoke in my lecture 'Christ, the Messenger', I emphasized that God exists in all great Messengers, including Christ, and that they are all manifestations of the same Infinite God.[1] I explained that the life of Christ represents the life of the past, and that every soul carries the past of the race within them through heredity, surroundings, and education.[2] I stated that we must worship Jesus Christ, the human manifestation of God, not an abstract God, as He is the only way to see and understand the Father.[3] I argued that it is not wrong to worship these man-Gods, as they embody a higher ideal of God than any abstract conception we may have.[4] I described Christ as a sign-post in the march of humanity, a giant who embodies the past and stretches out his hands for the future.[2] I noted that the wave of activity and repose in the march of events is a natural part of the universe, with rises and falls necessary for progress.[5] I emphasized that the message of Christ, 'Be ready, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand,' is a call to action and preparation for the final event.[6]

question: What did you say about Mohammedanism and Islam?

result.text: I spoke about Mohammedanism in my lecture on the way to the realisation of a universal religion, noting that all old religions, including Mohammedanism, have kept their mission intact despite their mistakes and difficulties.[1] I highlighted the practical brotherhood of all followers in Mohammedanism, stating that Islam makes its followers all equal, unlike other religions where people of different backgrounds may not kneel side by side to pray.[1] I acknowledged that Mohammedanism in India is quite different from that in other countries, as it is only when Mohammedans come from other countries and preach to their co-religionists in India about living with men who are not of their faith that a Mohammedan mob is aroused and fights.[2] I wrote to Akhandananda that Mohammedan boys must be admitted, but their religion should not be tampered with, and that the only thing needed is to make separate arrangements for their food and teach them to be moral, manly, and devoted to doing good to others.[3] In my lecture on the great teachers of the world, I noted that Mohammed was the Messenger of equality and that Mohammedanism has survived because of the good in its teaching, which includes the brotherhood of man and the brotherhood of all Mussulmans.[4] I pointed out that Mohammed by his life showed that amongst Mohammedans there should be perfect equality and brotherhood, regardless of race, caste, creed, colour, or sex.[5] I argued that the Vedantic spirit of religious liberality has affected Mohammedanism, and that Mohammedanism in India is quite a different thing from that in any other country.[2]

question: What were your views on the Vedas and their authority?

result.text: I argued that the Vedas are not the utterance of any person, but eternal knowledge that has always existed.[1] I stated that the Vedas do not owe their authority to any personal being, but are themselves the authority, being eternal knowledge of God.[1] I explained that the Rishis were spiritual discoverers who saw thoughts that already existed in the universe eternally.[1] I emphasized that the authority of the Vedas extends to all ages, climes, and persons, meaning their application is not confined to any particular place, time, or person.[2] I noted that only those portions of the Vedas which agree with reason are to be accepted as authority, while other Shâstras are only to be accepted so far as they do not go against the Vedas.[3] I clarified that the correct meaning of the statement 'The Vedas are beginningless and eternal' is that the law or truth revealed by them to man is permanent and changeless.[4] I stated that the Vedas are the eternal knowledge through which God created the world and that they talk high philosophy — the highest — and make this tremendous claim.[5] I said that the Vedas are a sort of incarnation of universal knowledge, and that the proof of God is that He brought forth the Vedas, and the proof of the Vedas is that such wonderful books could only have been given out by Brahman.[6]

question: What did you say about the Sikhs and Guru Govind Singh?

result.text: As I told Sharatchandra Chakravarty during our conversation, I spoke of Guru Govind Singh and his great renunciation, austerities, fortitude, and life-consecrating labours that brought about the revival of the Sikh sect.[1] I explained that Guru Govind Singh united both Hindus and Mussulmans within the fold of his religion and led them both towards the same end, an example unique in Indian history.[2] I emphasized that Guru Govind Singh did not create any common interest, but only pointed it out to the masses, and so both Hindus and Mussulmans followed him.[3] I recited a popular Dohâ of the Sikhs, which states that when Guru Govind gives the Name, a single man becomes strong enough to triumph over a lakh and a quarter of his foes.[4] In my lecture on the Common Bases of Hinduism, I praised Guru Govind Singh as an example of love and sacrifice, even when deserted by those for whom this blood was shed, retiring into the South to die like a wounded lion without a word of curse.[5] I noted that Guru Govind Singh was a great worshipper of Shakti, and that such an example of uniting Hindus and Mussulmans is indeed very rare in Indian history.[3] I also mentioned that Guru Govind Singh was one of the most glorious heroes of our race, who after shedding his blood and that of his dearest and nearest for the cause of religion, retired into the South to die like a wounded lion.[6]

question: What did you write to Sister Nivedita about her work for Indian women?

result.text: I wrote to Sister Nivedita from The Math on April 4, 1901, expressing my gladness to learn from a person of her authority of the good work she was doing in England.[1] I joined in earnest prayer with the hopes I entertained of her future services to India by her pen.[1] I wrote to Sister Nivedita from The Math on April 4, 1901, encouraging her to stay as long as she thought she was working well.[2] I mentioned that Yum had some talk about her with Mother, and that Mother desired her to come over.[2] I explained that it was only Mother's love and anxiety to see her that motivated the request.[2] I expressed my gladness that it should happen, as I had learned so much about her work from Mr. Dutt.[2]

question: What did you say about vegetarianism and meat-eating?

result.text: I wrote that to eat meat is surely barbarous and vegetable food is certainly purer — who can deny that?[1] I argued that for him surely is a strict vegetarian diet whose one end is to lead solely a spiritual life.[1] I stated that he who has to steer the boat of his life with strenuous labour through the constant life-and-death struggles and the competition of this world must of necessity take meat.[1] I taught meat-eating throughout the length and breadth of India in the hope that we can build a militant spirit![2] I said that in the West, the contention is whether animal food is injurious to health or not, whether it is more strengthening than vegetable diet or not, and so on.[3] I remarked that we are vegetarians — most of our diseases are of the stomach; our old men and women generally die of stomach complaints.[4] I explained that it is often stated that because Hindus believe in transmigration of souls they would not kill and eat animals because they feared that they would eat some of their ancestors.[5]

question: What was your opinion of social reformers in India?

result.text: Most of them are good, well-meaning men, and their aims too are very laudable on certain points.[1] I must frankly tell you that I am neither a caste-breaker nor a mere social reformer.[1] I have nothing to do directly with your castes or with your social reformation.[1] It is love and love alone that I preach, and I base my teaching on the great Vedantic truth of the sameness and omnipresence of the Soul of the Universe.[1] I have nothing to do directly with your castes or with your social reformation.[1] It is in the denunciation itself.[1] I am sorry to say that most of our modern reform movements have been inconsiderate imitations of Western means and methods of work; and that surely will not do for India.[1]

question: What did you say about the Theosophists?

result.text: I wrote to my brave boys that the Theosophical magazines claiming they prepared the way to my success is pure nonsense.[1] I remarked that the Theosophists claim to possess the original divine knowledge of the universe, and we are glad they mean to keep it a secret.[2] I told Mrs. Bull that in India, Theosophists and Buddhists are nonentities, only making a splash to catch Occidental ears.[3] I wrote to Alasinga that the Theosophists here like me, but they are only 650 in number, and I work with them but do not join any.[4] I noted that the Theosophists are having a jubilee time, and several press-notices are before us of their goings and doings for the last twenty-five years.[5] I remarked that Theosophy is the best serum we know of, whose injection never fails to develop the queer moths finding lodgment in some brains attempting to pass muster as sound.[6] I wrote that the Theosophists have not much power, but they are dead set against the orthodox section.[7] I remarked that the Theosophists wanted to crawl into the heart of Western Society, catching on to the skirts of scholars like Max Müller and poets like Edwin Arnold, all the same denouncing these very men and posing as the only receptacles of universal wisdom.[8]

question: What did you say about the English and British rule in India?

result.text: I wrote to Miss Mary Hale from Ridgely Manor on October 30, 1899, that despite the centuries of anarchy, massacres, and famines caused by British rule, there has been a good increase of population in India.[1] I noted that Indian labour and produce could support five times as many people as there are now in India with comfort, if the whole thing is not taken off from them.[1] I observed that the English public is forming the idea that the passing away of the Indian Empire from their sway will end in imminent peril to the English nation, and be their ruin.[2] I remarked that the way to maintain British supremacy in India is by keeping uppermost in the heart of every Indian the mighty prestige and glory of the British nation.[2] I pointed out that the Englishmen resident in India are forgetting that so long as the fortitude, perseverance, and national unity of purpose of the Englishmen are not eliminated from their national life, their throne in India is unshakable.[2] I argued that if the flow of the stream of those qualities is retarded, an Empire cannot be governed by the mere emblazoning of British prestige and glory.[2] I stated that when such remarkable traits of character are still predominant in the English as a nation, it is utterly useless to spend so much energy and power for the mere preservation of meaningless 'prestige'.[2]

question: What did you tell Mrs. Bull about your plans for the Math at Belur?

result.text: I wrote to Mrs. Bull from Murree that she has given much of the money and has implicit confidence in Sharat.[1] I told Mrs. Bull that I was going to see the new Math with Shri Mother and that Nivedita would preside at 6 p.m. that day.[2] I informed Mrs. Bull that I was in Benaras for a few days and that all letters should be addressed to the Belur Math.[3] I wrote to Mrs. Bull from Dacca that Mrs. Sevier was staying at Belur as the guest of Mrs. Banerjey.[4] I told Mrs. Bull that I was in the vale of death and that I was in Calcutta for rest and quiet due to my illness.[5]

question: What did you write about the historical evolution of India?

result.text: I wrote that the ancient history of India is full of descriptions of the gigantic energies and their multifarious workings, the boundless spirit, the combination of indomitable action and reaction of the various forces, and, above all, the profound thoughtfulness of a godly race.[1] I noted that the Vedas are the common source of Hinduism in all its varied stages, as also of Buddhism and every other religious belief in India.[2] I explained that the seeds of the multifarious growth of Indian thought on religion lie buried in the Vedas, and that Buddhism and the rest of India's religious thought are the outcome of the unfolding and expansion of those seeds.[2] I wrote that the northern reaction of ritualism was followed by the fitful glory of the Malava empire, and that northern India went to sleep for a long period before being rudely awakened by the thundering onrush of Mohammedan cavalry across the passes of Afghanistan.[3] I stated that the southern part of India experienced a spiritual upheaval with the teachings of Shankara and Ramanuja, followed by the usual Indian sequence of united races and powerful empires.[3] I wrote that the law of causation is omnipotent and knows no time or place when it did not exist, a doctrine as old as the Aryan race, sung by its ancient poet-seers, formulated by its philosophers, and made the corner-stone upon which the Hindu man even of today builds his whole scheme of life.[4]

question: How did you describe the Sannyasin's ideal in your poem?

result.text: I described the Sannyasin's ideal in my poem as one who has no home, with the sky as their roof and the grass as their bed.[1] I urged the Sannyasin to renounce all life, heavens, and hells, and to say 'Om Tat Sat, Om!' as a declaration of their liberation.[2] I emphasized that the Sannyasin must conquer their own self to conquer all, and never yield to the thirst for life.[3] I called upon the Sannyasin to cut their bonds and renounce all hopes and fears, saying 'Om Tat Sat, Om!' as a symbol of their spiritual awakening.[2] I told the Sannyasin that the Self is all in all, and that they are that very Self, saying 'Om Tat Sat, Om!' as a reminder of their true nature.[4] I urged the Sannyasin to let go of their hold on the world and to cease lamenting, saying 'Om Tat Sat, Om!' as a call to liberation.[5] I encouraged the Sannyasin to go beyond pain and pleasure, and to help others out of the veil of Maya, saying 'Om Tat Sat, Om!' as a declaration of their freedom.[6]

question: What did you say to your brother disciples about organising the Ramakrishna Mission?

result.text: I wrote to the brother-disciples at Alambazar Monastery, encouraging them to make an organised plan and to use tools like cameras, maps, and globes to educate the poor and ignorant.[1] I urged them to go from door to door, in the evening or at noon, to open the eyes of the people and teach them about Shri Ramakrishna and the world.[1] I told them that books alone would not suffice, but oral teaching would be more effective in reaching the people.[1] I also encouraged them to start associations in towns and villages where people revered Shri Ramakrishna and to gradually absorb other groups like the Hari Sabhâs.[2] I asked them if they could do all this or if they would only be content with bell-ringing, emphasizing the need for action and service.[1] I also mentioned the importance of having a big hut and gathering a number of poor, indigent folk to begin their work.[1]

question: What did you say about Shankaracharya and Advaita?

result.text: I spoke about Shankaracharya and Advaita in several lectures, where I pointed out that even great commentators like Shankaracharya, Râmânujâchârya, and Madhvâchârya had committed mistakes in interpreting the Upanishads.[1] I explained that Shankaracharya mistakenly believed that the whole of the Upanishads taught only Advaitism, and he twisted the meaning of passages that bore the Dvaita idea to support his own theory.[1] I noted that the followers of Shankaracharya hold that the soul is Vibhu, omnipresent, while the followers of Ramanuja believe it is Anu, like a particle, very small.[2] I emphasized that the Advaita system existed ages before Shankara was born, and he was one of its last representatives.[3] I stated that the real essence of Buddhism and that of the Vedanta are not very different, but that the disciples did not understand the Master and have degraded themselves, denying the existence of the soul and of God.[4] I mentioned that Shankaracharya realising that state has said, 'Where is the universe vanished?' and so on, showing his own experience of Oneness.[5] I argued that the Upanishads have been taken up by every sect in India that wants to claim authority for orthodoxy, and that all these systems are covered by the word Vedanta.[3]

question: What did you say about Ramanuja and qualified non-dualism?

result.text: I explained that Ramanuja is the leading dualistic philosopher of later India, whom all the other dualistic sects have followed, directly or indirectly, both in the substance of their teaching and in the organization of their sects even down to some of the most minute points of their organization.[1] I noted that according to Ramanuja, these three entities are eternal — God, and soul, and nature.[2] I stated that the system of Ramanuja admits the unity of the total, within that totality of existence there are, according to him, eternal differences.[3] I mentioned that the qualified non-dualists express it more beautifully than the dualists, by saying that the soul's purity and perfection become contracted and again become manifest, and what we are now trying to do is to remanifest the intelligence, the purity, the power which is natural to the soul.[4] I emphasized that the Advaita is not antagonistic to the Dvaita (dualism), and that the latter is only one of three steps in the spiritual journey.[5] I explained that the Vedanta philosophy includes three systems of philosophy and sects — one is the dualistic, or Dvaita; a second is the qualified non-dualistic, or Vishishtâdvaita; and a third is the non-dualistic, or Advaita.[6]

question: What did you say about the Buddha as a person?

result.text: I said that Buddha stood head and shoulders above all other men.[1][2] I said that his friends or enemies could never say that he drew a breath or ate a crumb of bread but for the good of all.[1][2] I said that Buddha was one of the greatest human beings, who gave to the world a complete system of morality.[3] I said that he was born for the good of men, and that his only concern was how to help others in misery.[4] I said that he was more brave and sincere than any teacher, and that he repudiated the idea of God as something external.[3][5] I said that he taught that there is no God, only man himself, and that man has infinite power within himself.[5] I said that he was the first human being to give to the world a complete system of morality, and that he was good for good's sake.[3] I said that he was the most tremendous religious movement that the world ever saw, and that its effect has been felt in every civilisation.[6]

question: What did you say about the role of the Brahmin in India's future?

result.text: I argued that the Brahmin must work for the salvation of the rest of mankind in India, and if he does that, he remains a true Brahmin.[1] I stated that the Brahmin must open the treasury of virtue and distribute its valuables to the world, as he was the earliest preacher to the Indian races.[1] I emphasized that the Brahmin must not occupy himself with any secular business and must not receive gifts from everybody, as this is the life of a truly orthodox Brahmin.[2] I pointed out that the Brahmin must give to the people at large the accumulated culture of ages, and it was because he did not do so that the Mohammedan invasion was possible.[3] I said that the Brahmin must be the first to break open the cells that hide the wonderful treasures accumulated by our common ancestors and give them to everybody.[3] I noted that the Brahmin must not be allowed to remain in his exclusive privileges and exclusive claims, as the days of such privileges are gone forever from the soil of India.[1] I explained that the Brahmin must be the ideal of humanity in India, as wonderfully put forward by Shankaracharya, and that he must remain as the man of God, the ideal man, the perfect man.[4]

question: What did you say about American women?

result.text: I praised the American women most enthusiastically, noting their kindness and the role they play in every movement in this country.[1] I remarked on the absence of poverty in America, especially in relation to the American women.[2] I stated that nowhere on earth have women so many privileges as in America, and that the number of cultured women is much greater than that of cultured men.[3] I observed that the average American woman is far more cultivated than the average American man, and that they snatch every opportunity to improve themselves.[4] I noted that in America, women are the life of every movement and represent all the culture of the nation, for men are too busy to educate themselves.[1] I said that in America, women are more learned than men, and that they are all well versed in science and philosophy.[5] I expressed my gratitude for the kindness of the American women, and I cannot express my gratitude for their kindness.[1]

question: What did you say about the Jains?

result.text: I wrote to Mrs. Bull from Chicago that I lectured at Brooklyn last Sunday, and some of the prominent members of the Ethical Society including Dr. Jain were there.[1] I told the audience at the Unitarian church that the Jains show remarkable kindness to dumb animals, and whose moral law is summed up in the words: 'Not to injure others is the highest good.'[2] I explained that the Jains were the first great ascetics, and that they elaborated the principle of non-injury and doing good throughout their teachings.[3] I noted that the Jains were a conservative force in India, and that they declared against the validity of the scriptures of the Hindus, the Vedas, claiming that their own books were the only original Vedas.[4] I mentioned that there were several millions of Jains in India, and that their priests and monks tied a handkerchief over their faces believing that if their hot breath came in contact with man or beast death would ensue.[5] I pointed out that the Jains were a sect that believed in a soul, but were agnostic in relation to God, and that they were a significant religious group in India.[5] I observed that the Jains were a sect that believed in the soul, but not in the moral government of the country, and that they were a significant religious group in India.[5]

question: What did you write about the Paris Congress of the History of Religions?

result.text: I wrote that the Congress of the History of Religions at Paris was attended only by scholars who devote themselves to the study of the origin and the history of different religions.[1] I noted that the Congress was not a big affair, with only some twenty scholars discussing topics like the origin of the Shâlagrâma and Jehovah.[2] I mentioned that the Congress of the History of Religions was like the Congress of Orientalists, with European scholars versed in Oriental languages meeting.[3] I stated that the substance of the lecture would be printed in French in the General Report of the Congress.[4] I observed that the Congress was not intended to discuss the doctrines or spiritual views of any religion, but rather to inquire into the historic evolution of established faiths.[1] I pointed out that the Roman Catholics, who had previously organised the Chicago Parliament of Religions, were now opposing the repetition of any such gathering.[1] I noted that France, being a Roman Catholic country, prevented the convening of a religious congress due to the opposition from the Roman Catholic world.[1]

question: What did you say about the Vedanta being practical?

result.text: I have been asked to say something about the practical position of the Vedanta philosophy.[1] As I have told you, theory is very good indeed, but how are we to carry it into practice?[1] The Vedanta, therefore, as a religion must be intensely practical.[1] We must be able to carry it out in every part of our lives.[1] The ideals of religion must cover the whole field of life, they must enter into all our thoughts, and more and more into practice.[1] The Vedanta preaches the ideal; and the ideal, as we know, is always far ahead of the real, of the practical, as we may call it.[2] It is a great thing to understand this, for the former tendency is the temptation of our lives.[2] The Vedanta teaches men to have faith in themselves first.[2] The Vedanta also says that not only can this be realised in the depths of forests or caves, but by men in all possible conditions of life.[3] Religion, to help mankind, must be ready and able to help him in whatever condition he is, in servitude or in freedom, in the depths of degradation or on the heights of purity; everywhere, equally, it should be able to come to his aid.[4]

question: What did you say about Kali and Mother worship?

result.text: I wrote to Swami Brahmananda from the U.S.A. on 1899-11-20 that on this sacred day to the Divine Mother, may the Mother dance in your hearts and bring infinite strength to your arms.[1] I blessed you all and declared that Mother will certainly come down with great strength to bring all victory, world victory.[1] I told the disciple that the figure of Mother Kali represents the union of the blissful and the terrible aspects, though no picture can adequately express these.[2] I performed a Homa before the Mother Kali at Kalighat and was glad to see the liberality of view there, as the temple authorities did not object to my worship.[3] I explained that Kali worship is not a necessary step in any religion, and that the Upanishads teach us all there is of religion.[4] I stated that I believe in a great Power that thinks of Herself as feminine, called Kali and Mother, and also in Brahman.[5] I emphasized that Kali worship is my special fad, but I only preach what is good for universal humanity.[4]

question: What did you say about the hymn 'As the different streams having their sources in different places'?

result.text: I quoted to you, brethren, a few lines from a hymn which I remember to have repeated from my earliest boyhood, which is every day repeated by millions and millions of human beings: 'As the different streams having their sources in different places all mingle their water in the sea, so, O Lord, the different paths which men take through different tendencies, various though they appear, crooked or straight, all lead to Thee.'[1] I will quote to you, brothers, a few lines from a hymn which every Hindoo child repeats every day.[2] As the different streams, having their sources in different places, all mingle their water in the sea; O Lord, so the different paths which men take through different tendencies, various though they appear, crooked or straight, all lead to Thee.[2] As so many rivers, having their source in different mountains, roll down, crooked or straight, and at last come into the ocean — so, all these various creeds and religions, taking their start from different standpoints and running through crooked or straight courses, at last come unto THEE.[3]

question: What did you say about the Gita and Krishna's historicity?

result.text: As I discussed in my lecture on the Gita, the book forms a part of the Mahâbhârata, and several things are very important to know in order to understand it properly.[1] I noted that it is human nature to build round the real character of a great man all sorts of imaginary superhuman attributes, and that Krishna may have been a king.[2] I pointed out that the style of language of the Gita is the same as that of the Mahabharata, and that the line of thought in the Gita is the same as in the Mahabharata.[3] I mentioned that Krishna was a married man and that there are thousands of books about him, but I do not find them particularly interesting.[4] I stated that the Gita harmonizes all these conflicting doctrines, and that whether or not Krishna ever lived, I do not know.[5] I remarked that the Gita is not Krishna's only sermon, and that the central idea in Krishna's life is non-attachment.[4]

question: How did you define religion in your lectures?

result.text: As I explained in my lecture on 'What Is Religion?', religion is the realisation of the Divinity already in man.[1] In my lecture on 'What Is Religion?', I said that religion is not merely talk or belief, but the realisation of the Universal, where one sees God in every person and feels the oneness of all existence.[2] I argued that religion is the realisation of Spirit as Spirit, not as matter.[3] In my lecture on 'What Is Religion?', I stated that religion is the highest spiritual worship, where one worships the Infinite through the spirit, not through limited forms.[2] I explained that religion is not a matter of doctrines or theories, but a transformation of one's whole nature into the truth.[4] In my lecture on 'What Is Religion?', I said that religion is the manifestation of the Divinity already in man, and that it is not limited to any one form or tradition.[1] I stated that religion is the realisation of the Universal, where one sees God in every being and feels the oneness of all existence.[2]

question: What did you say about the problem of evil?

result.text: I spoke about the problem of evil in my lecture on 'Worshipper and Worshipped', where I explained that the only way to solve the problem is by saying that God is the cause of both good and evil.[1] I argued that if you say God is only good and not evil, you will be caught in the trap of your own argument.[1] I stated that the same difficulty arises when you say God is the Father of this universe and good, yet there is also evil in the world, implying God must be evil.[1] In my lecture on 'Discipleship', I emphasized that good and evil always exist in the world, and many try to forget or deny the presence of evil.[2] I pointed out that denying the existence of evil is also a weakness, stemming from a fear of it.[2] I explained that God has put evil in the world, but we do not have to whitewash Him, and why there is evil is none of our business.[2] In my notes on 'Mother-Worship', I criticized the view of absolute separation of good and evil, calling it a brutal view that leads to jealousy and hatred.[3]

question: What did you say about hypnotism and psychic powers?

result.text: I argued that the Western concept of hypnotism is only a part of the real thing, and that the Hindus call it self-hypnotisation.[1] I stated that the soul cannot have any sex, and that the idea of a man or a woman in the soul is a form of self-hypnotism.[2] I warned that the great danger of psychic powers is that they are used without proper training, leading to abnormal rousing of sexual feelings.[3] I explained that the Advaitist alone does not care to be hypnotised, and that his system understands that hypnotism comes with every form of dualism.[1] I said that the study of higher psychology has been retarded in the West by being identified with mere alleged psychic phenomena.[4] I pointed out that every other religion that preaches these things as real is practicing a form of hypnotism.[1] I noted that the Advaitist says to throw away even the Vedas, the Personal God, the universe, and one's own body and mind to get rid of hypnotism perfectly.[1]

question: What did you tell the Alambazar Math members about rules of the monastery?

result.text: I wrote to the members of the Alambazar Math from High View on April 27, 1896, emphasizing the importance of rules and regulations for the monastery.[1] I explained that it is necessary at the immature stage to be guided by rules, as the Master used to say that the sapling must be hedged round.[1] I warned against feelings of jealousy or egotism gaining ground among the members, as they could hinder the well-being of the world.[1] I encouraged them to contribute to the great well-being of the world, though many may not yet be aware of it.[1] I also mentioned that it is natural for idle minds to indulge in gossip and faction-mongering, and thus provided some hints to avoid such pitfalls.[1]

question: What did you say about Mahavira and Indian history?

result.text: I spoke about Mahavira and Indian history in a conversation where I emphasized the importance of making Mahavira's character an ideal for the people.[1] I mentioned that Mahavira, like Rama, was a perfect master of his senses and wonderfully sagacious, and that his whole-hearted devotion was essential for personal service.[1] I urged the people to build their lives on the great ideal of personal service, which would gradually manifest other ideals in life.[1] I stressed the importance of obedience to the Guru without questioning and strict observance of Brahmacharya as the secret of success.[1] I criticized the degeneration of Indian culture due to the prevalence of light tunes like Kheâl and Tappâ, which I believed had converted the country into a land of women.[1] I called for the revival of the austere spirit of heroic manhood through the use of martial music and the chanting of 'Mahavira, Mahavira' and 'Hara, Hara, Vyom, Vyom'.[1]

citations.citation: [Vol 7, Conversations and Dialogues, Sharat Chandra Chakravarty]

question: What did you write about the East and the West in your essay?

result.text: I wrote that both the East and the West are good, and neither can be praised nor blamed over the other, as both scales are equal.[1] I noted that in the West, ideas of decency and etiquette vary according to different countries, such as the English and Americans having one type, the French another, and the Germans yet another.[2] I observed that the East and the West have different ideals, with the East focusing on producing perfect individuals through Sannyasa and concentration, while the West aims at perfecting the social state.[3] I mentioned that there is more chance of working out my plans in the East than in the West, as it now appears.[4] I suggested that the future may hold the conjunction of the East and the West, which could lead to marvellous results.[5]

question: What did you say about the Arya Samaj and Dayananda?

result.text: I wrote that the Arya Samaj, founded by Swami Dayânanda Sarasvati, is one of the sects that have been useless mixtures, merely voices of apology to our English masters to allow us to live.[1] I noted that the Arya Samaj, along with the Brahmo Samaj, has been a voice of apology to our English masters, and that we have started a new India — a growth — waiting to see what comes.[1] I mentioned that the Arya Samaj, like the Brahmo Samaj, has been a voice of apology to our English masters, and that we believe in new ideas only when the nation wants them, and what will be true for us.[1] I wrote that the Arya Samaj, along with the Brahmo Samaj, has been a voice of apology to our English masters, and that the test of truth for this Brahmo Samaj is 'what our masters approve'; with us, what the Indian reasoning and experience approves.[1] I wrote that the Arya Samaj, along with the Brahmo Samaj, has been a voice of apology to our English masters, and that the struggle has begun — not between the Brahmo Samaj and us, for they are gone already, but a harder, deeper, and more terrible one.[1]

question: What did you say about Tantra and the Tantras?

result.text: I have no faith in the theories advanced by Western savants with regard to the Vedas.[1] However, about the Puranas, I have told you that they are authoritative only in so far as they agree with the Vedas, otherwise not.[1] In the Puranas we find many things which do not agree with the Vedas.[1] As for instance, it is written in the Puranas that some one lived ten thousand years, another twenty thousand years, but in the Vedas we find: — 'Man lives indeed a hundred years.'[1] Certainly the Vedas.[1] Notwithstanding statements like these, I do not depreciate the Puranas.[1] They contain many beautiful and illuminating teachings and words of wisdom on Yoga, Bhakti, Jnâna, and Karma; those, of course, we should accept.[1]

question: What did you say about spiritualism and talking to the dead?

result.text: I wrote to the editor of Light that the truth of correspondence between the living and the dead is in every religion, and nowhere more than in the Vedantic sects of India, where the fact of mutual help between the departed and the living has been made the basis of the law of inheritance.[1] I told the audience at the lecture on Formal Worship that there was one of those ladies who bring the departed spirits down to us — a medium, and that she was very large, yet she was called medium.[2] I remarked that I had a very peculiar experience during a seance, where the medium said she saw a ghost standing there, and the ghost told her that there was a Hindu gentleman on that bench, but I stood up and said, 'It required no ghost to tell you that.'[2] I wrote to my brother-disciples in New York that there are a good many spiritualists in this country, and that the medium is one who induces the spirit, and that I have witnessed some cases, but they seemed to be a hoax.[3] I told the audience at the lecture on Is Vedanta the Future Religion? that I have attended several spiritualistic meetings, and that in one, the leader was a woman who said to me, 'Your mother and grandfather came to me,' but I pointed out that my mother is living yet.[4] I wrote to the editor of Light that I would be very sorry if I were mistaken as antagonistic to any sect or form of religion, so far as they are sincere, and that I do not hold that any system can ever be judged by the frauds and failures that would naturally gather round every method under the present circumstances.[1] I remarked that I think people really are atheists, just the desire for these five senses, not satisfied with what they have here, they want more of the same when they die.[4]

question: What did you say about the poverty of your own family?

result.text: I wrote to Maharaja Ajit Singh that after trying a different climate for two years, I was getting worse every day and now almost at death's door.[1] I told him that I have one great sin rankling always in my breast, and that is to do a service to the world, I have sadly neglected my mother.[1] I mentioned that since my second brother has gone away, my mother has become awfully worn-out with grief.[1] I expressed my desire to make Sevâ and serve my mother for some years at least, and to live with her and get my younger brother married to prevent extinction of the family.[1] I told him that my mother lives now in a hovel and I want to build a little, decent home for her and make some provision for the youngest.[1] I wrote to Marie Halboister that the greatest misery in my life has been my own people — my brothers and sisters and mother etc.[2] I told her that relatives are like deadly clogs to one's progress, and it is a wonder that people will still go on to find new ones by marriage.[2]

question: What did you say about the Chicago Fair and your early days in America?

result.text: As I told the interviewer in London, I represented the Hindu religion at the Parliament of Religions held at Chicago in 1893.[1] I described the Chicago Fair as a tremendous affair, requiring at least ten days to go through it.[2] I mentioned that I remained about twelve days in Chicago and almost every day I used to go to the Fair.[2] I recounted how the Raja of Kapurthala was being lionised by some portion of Chicago society, but I was too big to speak with a poor Fakir.[3] I noted that the eccentric Mahratta Brâhmin selling nail-made pictures in the Fair told the reporters all sorts of things against the Raja.[3] I explained that the newspaper editors wanted to give the boy's stories some weight, and the next day they wrote huge columns in their papers about the description of a man of wisdom from India, meaning me.[3] I mentioned that the American people have proved most interested audiences and sympathetic friends, and my work there has so taken root that I must shortly return to that country.[1]

question: What did you say about your health and illness in your last years?

result.text: I wrote to Sister Christine from The Math that I was once more in the vale of death, with the old diabetes having disappeared but replaced by asthma or dyspepsia due to nervous prostration.[1] I told Sister Christine from Suez that I was very ill in India, with my heart going wrong due to mountain climbing, glacier water bathing, and nervous prostration, and that I had terrible asthma fits lasting seven days and nights.[2] I wrote to Sister Christine from The Math that I was very anxious about her health and had not received any letters from her for a long time.[3] I wrote to Sister Christine from Ridgely Manor that I was very anxious to know how she was and asked her to write a line to tell me she was in very good health.[4] I wrote to Miss Mary Hale from Ridgely Manor that I had arrived and was hoping to see Isabelle and Harriet, though Harriet had been uniformly silent.[5] I wrote to Miss Mary Hale from The Math that my health was getting worse every day, with many complications and botherations, and that I had ceased to notice it at all.[6] I wrote to Sister Christine from The Math that I was sleeping better and the general health was not bad.[7]

question: What did you say about music and art in India?

result.text: I spoke about how in India, music was developed to the full seven notes, even to half and quarter notes, ages ago, and that India led in music, also in drama and sculpture.[1] I explained that in India, drama and music are themselves held to be religion, and that any song, whether it be a love-song or otherwise, if one's whole soul is in that song, one attains salvation.[2] I noted that the music of the West is much advanced, with the sentiment of pathos as well as of heroism in their music, which is as it should be.[3] I mentioned that the Mohammedans took up the different Râgas and Râginis after coming into India, but they put such a stamp of their own colouring on the art of Tappa songs that all the science in music was destroyed.[4] I emphasized that in India, the art and science of music, as well as other arts, are deeply connected to the spiritual and philosophical ideals of the nation.[5] I observed that each nation has a characteristic of its own, and that in India, the expression of art is more rounded and wave-like, unlike the pointed and jerky expressions found in the West.[6] I pointed out that the music of India, particularly in Kirtana and Dhrupada, represents the real music we have, while the rest has been spoiled by being modulated according to the Islamic methods.[4]

question: What is Karma-Yoga?

result.text:
This is how I treated it in Karma-Yoga.
“The grandest idea in the religion of the Vedanta is that we may reach the same goal by different paths; and these paths I have generalised into four, viz those of work, love, psychology, and knowledge. But you must, at the same time, remember that these divisions are not very marked and quite exclusive of each other. Each blends into the other. But according to the type which prevails, we name the divisions. It is not that you can find men who have no other faculty than that of work, nor that you can find men who are no more than devoted worshippers only, nor that there are men who have no more than mere knowledge. These divisions are made in accordance with the type or the tendency that may be seen to prevail in a man. We have found that, in the end, all these four paths converge and become one. All religions and all methods of work and worship lead us to one and the same goal.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 7: Freedom]; [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 1: Karma in Its Effect on Character].

question: What is Raja-Yoga?

result.text:
In Raja-Yoga I set it down thus.
“So far, then, we see that in the study of this Raja-Yoga no faith or belief is necessary. Believe nothing until you find it out for yourself; that is what it teaches us. Truth requires no prop to make it stand. Do you mean to say that the facts of our awakened state require any dreams or imaginings to prove them? Certainly not. This study of Raja-Yoga takes a long time and constant practice. A part of this practice is physical, but in the main it is mental. As we proceed we shall find how intimately the mind is connected with the body. If we believe that the mind is simply a finer part of the body, and that mind acts upon the body, then it stands to reason that the body must react upon the mind. If the body is sick, the mind becomes sick also. If the body is healthy, the mind remains healthy and strong. When one is angry, the mind becomes disturbed. Similarly when the mind is disturbed, the body also becomes disturbed. With the majority of mankind the mind is greatly under the control of the body, their mind being very little developed. The vast mass of humanity is very little removed from the animals. Not only so, but in many instances, the power of control in them is little higher than that of the lower animals.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Preface]; [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Ch. 8: Raja-Yoga in Brief].

question: What is Bhakti-Yoga?

result.text:
In Bhakti-Yoga I set it down thus.
“He is the Soul of the Universe; He is Immortal; His is the Rulership; He is the All-knowing, the All-pervading, the Protector of the Universe, the Eternal Ruler. None else is there efficient to govern the world eternally. He who at the beginning of creation projected Brahmâ (i.e. the universal consciousness), and who delivered the Vedas unto him — seeking liberation I go for refuge unto that effulgent One, whose light turns the understanding towards the Âtman.” [1]

question: What is Jnana-Yoga?

result.text:
I put it this way in my address The First Step Towards Jnana.
“The word Jnâna means knowledge. It is derived from the root Jnâ — to know — the same word from which your English word to know is derived. Jnana-Yoga is Yoga by means of knowledge. What is the object of the Jnana-Yoga? Freedom. Freedom from what? Freedom from our imperfections, freedom from the misery of life. Why are we miserable? We are miserable because we are bound. What is the bondage? The bondage is of nature. Who is it that binds us?” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 6, Lectures and Discourses, Introduction to Jnana-Yoga]; [Vol 8, Lectures and Discourses, Jnana Yoga].

question: What is the secret of work?

result.text:
This is how I treated it in Karma-Yoga.
“What is Karma-Yoga? The knowledge of the secret of work. We see that the whole universe is working. For what? For salvation, for liberty; from the atom to the highest being, working for the one end, liberty for the mind, for the body, for the spirit. All things are always trying to get freedom, flying away from bondage. The sun, the moon, the earth, the planets, all are trying to fly away from bondage. The centrifugal and the centripetal forces of nature are indeed typical of our universe. Instead of being knocked about in this universe, and after long delay and thrashing, getting to know things as they are, we learn from Karma-Yoga the secret of work, the method of work, the organising power of work. A vast mass of energy may be spent in vain if we do not know how to utilise it. Karma-Yoga makes a science of work; you learn by it how best to utilise all the workings of this world. Work is inevitable, it must be so; but we should work to the highest purpose. Karma-Yoga makes us admit that this world is a world of five minutes, that it is a something we have to pass through; and that freedom is not here, but is only to be found beyond. To find the way out of the bondages of the world we have to go through it slowly and surely.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 3: The Secret of Work]; [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 1: Karma in Its Effect on Character].

question: What is duty?

result.text:
In Karma-Yoga I set it down thus.
“It is necessary in the study of Karma-Yoga to know what duty is. If I have to do something I must first know that it is my duty, and then I can do it. The idea of duty again is different in different nations. The Mohammedan says what is written in his book, the Koran, is his duty; the Hindu says what is in the Vedas is his duty; and the Christian says what is in the Bible is his duty. We find that there are varied ideas of duty, differing according to different states in life, different historical periods and different nations. The term "duty", like every other universal abstract term, is impossible clearly to define; we can only get an idea of it by knowing its practical operations and results. When certain things occur before us, we have all a natural or trained impulse to act in a certain manner towards them; when this impulse comes, the mind begins to think about the situation. Sometimes it thinks that it is good to act in a particular manner under the given conditions; at other times it thinks that it is wrong to act in the same manner even in the very same circumstances. The ordinary idea of duty everywhere is that every good man follows the dictates of his conscience. But what is it that makes an act a duty?” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 7: Freedom]; [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 2: Each Is Great in His Own Place].

question: What is Maya?

result.text:
I wrote of this in Jnana-Yoga, in the chapter Ch. 3: Maya and Illusion.
“Almost all of you have heard of the word Mâyâ. Generally it is used, though incorrectly, to denote illusion, or delusion, or some such thing. But the theory of Maya forms one of the pillars upon which the Vedanta rests; it is, therefore, necessary that it should be properly understood. I ask a little patience of you, for there is a great danger of its being misunderstood. The oldest idea of Maya that we find in Vedic literature is the sense of delusion; but then the real theory had not been reached. We find such passages as, "Indra through his Maya assumed various forms." Here it is true the word Maya means something like magic, and we find various other passages, always taking the same meaning. The word Maya then dropped out of sight altogether. But in the meantime the idea was developing. Later, the question was raised: "Why can't we know this secret of the universe?"” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 2, Jnana-Yoga, Ch. 4: Maya and the Evolution of the Conception of God]; [Vol 2, Jnana-Yoga, Ch. 5: Maya and Freedom].

question: What is Prana?

result.text:
This is how I treated it in Raja-Yoga.
“Prânâyâma is not, as many think, something about breath; breath indeed has very little to do with it, if anything. Breathing is only one of the many exercises through which we get to the real Pranayama. Pranayama means the control of Prâna. According to the philosophers of India, the whole universe is composed of two materials, one of which they call Âkâsha. It is the omnipresent, all-penetrating existence. Everything that has form, everything that is the result of combination, is evolved out of this Akasha. It is the Akasha that becomes the air, that becomes the liquids, that becomes the solids; it is the Akasha that becomes the sun, the earth, the moon, the stars, the comets; it is the Akasha that becomes the human body, the animal body, the plants, every form that we see, everything that can be sensed, everything that exists. It cannot be perceived; it is so subtle that it is beyond all ordinary perception; it can only be seen when it has become gross, has taken form. At the beginning of creation there is only this Akasha. At the end of the cycle the solids, the liquids, and the gases all melt into the Akasha again, and the next creation similarly proceeds out of this Akasha.” [1]

question: What is the goal of Raja-Yoga?

result.text:
I said this in a discourse, The Aim of Raja-Yoga, as my hearers noted it down.
“Yoga has essentially to do with the meditative side of religion, rather than the ethical side, though, of necessity, a little of the latter has to be considered. Men and women are growing to desire more than mere revelation, so called. They want facts in their own consciousness. Only through experience can there be any reality in religion. Spiritual facts are to be gathered mostly from the superconscious state of mind. Let us put ourselves into the same condition as did those who claim to have had special experiences; then if we have similar experiences, they become facts for us. We can see all that another has seen; a thing that happened once can happen again, nay, must, under the same circumstances. Raja-Yoga teaches us how to reach the superconscious state. All the great religions recognise this state in some form; but in India, special attention is paid to this side of religion. In the beginning, some mechanical means may help us to acquire this state; but mechanical means alone can never accomplish much. Certain positions, certain modes of breathing, help to harmonise and concentrate the mind, but with these must go purity and strong desire for God, or realisation.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 5, Notes from Lectures and Discourses, The Goal and Methods of Realisation].

question: How should I practise meditation?

result.text:
I spoke of this in a conversation that Sharatchandra Chakravarty wrote down.
“First, the practice of meditation has to proceed with some one object before the mind. Once I used to concentrate my mind on some black point. Ultimately, during those days, I could not see the point any more, nor notice that the point was before me at all — the mind used to be no more — no wave of functioning would rise, as if it were all an ocean without any breath of air. In that state I used to experience glimpses of supersensuous truth. So I think, the practice of meditation even with some trifling external object leads to mental concentration. But it is true that the mind very easily attains calmness when one practices meditation with anything on which one's mind is most apt to settle down. This is the reason why we have in this country so much worship of the images of gods and goddesses. And what wonderful art developed from such worship! But no more of that now. The fact, however, is that the objects of meditation can never be the same in the case of all men. People have proclaimed and preached to others only those external objects to which they held on to become perfected in meditation. Oblivious of the fact, later on, that these objects are aids to the attainment of perfect mental calmness, men have extolled them beyond everything else. They have wholly concerned themselves with the means, getting comparatively unmindful of the end.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 7, Conversations and Dialogues, Sharat Chandra Chakravarty].

question: What is the Atman?

result.text:
In Jnana-Yoga I set it down thus.
“According to the Advaita philosophy, there is only one thing real in the universe, which it calls Brahman; everything else is unreal, manifested and manufactured out of Brahman by the power of Mâyâ. To reach back to that Brahman is our goal. We are, each one of us, that Brahman, that Reality, plus this Maya. If we can get rid of this Maya or ignorance, then we become what we really are. According to this philosophy, each man consists of three parts — the body, the internal organ or the mind, and behind that, what is called the Âtman, the Self. The body is the external coating and the mind is the internal coating of the Atman who is the real perceiver, the real enjoyer, the being in the body who is working the body by means of the internal organ or the mind.” [1]

question: What is the real nature of man?

result.text:
I wrote of this in Jnana-Yoga, in the chapter Ch. 2: The Real Nature of Man.
“We are not individuals yet. We are struggling towards individuality, and that is the Infinite, that is the real nature of man. He alone lives whose life is in the whole universe, and the more we concentrate our lives on limited things, the faster we go towards death. Those moments alone we live when our lives are in the universe, in others; and living this little life is death, simply death, and that is why the fear of death comes. The fear of death can only be conquered when man realises that so long as there is one life in this universe, he is living. When he can say, "I am in everything, in everybody, I am in all lives, I am the universe," then alone comes the state of fearlessness. To talk of immortality in constantly changing things is absurd. Says an old Sanskrit philosopher: It is only the Spirit that is the individual, because it is infinite. No infinity can be divided; infinity cannot be broken into pieces. It is the same one, undivided unit for ever, and this is the individual man, the Real Man. The apparent man is merely a struggle to express, to manifest this individuality which is beyond; and evolution is not in the Spirit. These changes which are going on — the wicked becoming good, the animal becoming man, take them in whatever way you like — are not in the Spirit. They are evolution of nature and manifestation of Spirit.” [1]

question: What is the ideal of a universal religion?

result.text:
Here is what I said on this when I spoke on The Ideal of a Universal Religion.
“This is the existing condition of religion, the existing condition of things. What I want to propagate is a religion that will be equally acceptable to all minds; it must be equally philosophic, equally emotional, equally mystic, and equally conducive to action. If professors from the colleges come, scientific men and physicists, they will court reason. Let them have it as much as they want. There will be a point beyond which they will think they cannot go, without breaking with reason. They will say, "These ideas of God and salvation are superstitious, guise them up! " I say, "Mr. Philosopher, this body of yours is a bigger superstition. Give it up, don't go home to dinner or to your philosophic chair. Give up the body, and if you cannot, cry quarter and sit down." For religion must be able to show how to realise the philosophy that teaches us that this world is one, that there is but one Existence in the universe. Similarly, if the mystic comes, we must welcome him, be ready to give him the science of mental analysis, and practically demonstrate it before him. And if emotional people come, we must sit, laugh, and weep with them in the name of the Lord; we must "drink the cup of love and become mad". If the energetic worker comes, we must work with him, with all the energy that we have.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 2, Practical Vedanta and Other Lectures, The Way to the Realisation of a Universal Religion].

question: What is the difference between religion and the religions?

result.text:
I put it this way in my address The Methods and Purpose of Religion.
“In studying the religions of the world we generally find two methods of procedure. The one is from God to man. That is to say, we have the Semitic group of religions in which the idea of God comes almost from the very first, and, strangely enough, without any idea of soul. It was very remarkable amongst the ancient Hebrews that, until very recent periods in their history, they never evolved any idea of a human soul. Man was composed of certain mind and material particles, and that was all. With death everything ended. But, on the other hand, there was a most wonderful idea of God evolved by the same race. This is one of the methods of procedure. The other is through man to God. The second is peculiarly Aryan, and the first is peculiarly Semitic.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 6, Lectures and Discourses, The Vedanta Philosophy and Christianity]; [Vol 3, Lectures and Discourses, Unity, the Goal of Religion].

question: What is renunciation?

result.text:
This is how I treated it in Raja-Yoga.
“The two motive powers of our actions are (1) what we see ourselves, (2) the experience of others. These two forces throw the mind, the lake, into various waves. Renunciation is the power of battling against these forces and holding the mind in check. Their renunciation is what see want. I am passing through a street, and a man comes and takes away my watch. That is my own experience. I see it myself, and it immediately throws my Chitta into a wave, taking the form of anger. Allow not that to come. If you cannot prevent that, you are nothing; if you can, you have Vairâgya. Again, the experience of the worldly-minded teaches us that sense-enjoyments are the highest ideal. These are tremendous temptations. To deny them, and not allow the mind to come to a wave form with regard to them, is renunciation; to control the twofold motive powers arising from my own experience and from the experience of others, and thus prevent the Chitta from being governed by them, is Vairagya. These should be controlled by me, and not I by them. This sort of mental strength is called renunciation. Vairagya is the only way to freedom.” [1]

question: What is Para-Bhakti?

result.text:
This is how I treated it in Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion.
“The higher knowledge is thus clearly shown to be the knowledge of the Brahman; and the Devi-Bhâgavata gives us the following definition of the higher love (Para-Bhakti): "As oil poured from one vessel to another falls in an unbroken line, so, when the mind in an unbroken stream thinks of the Lord, we have what is called Para-Bhakti or supreme love." This kind of undisturbed and ever-steady direction of the mind and the heart to the Lord with an inseparable attachment is indeed the highest manifestation of man's love to God. All other forms of Bhakti are only preparatory to the attainment of this highest form thereof, viz the Para-Bhakti which is also known as the love that comes after attachment (Râgânugâ). When this supreme love once comes into the heart of man, his mind will continuously think of God and remember nothing else. He will give no room in himself to thoughts other than those of God, and his soul will be unconquerably pure and will alone break all the bonds of mind and matter and become serenely free. He alone can worship the Lord in his own heart; to him forms, symbols, books, and doctrines are all unnecessary and are incapable of proving serviceable in any way. It is not easy to love the Lord thus. Ordinarily human love is seen to flourish only in places where it is returned; where love is not returned for love, cold indifference is the natural result.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 3, Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion, Ch. 1: The Preparatory Renunciation]; [Vol 3, Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion, Ch. 2: The Bhakta's Renunciation Results from Love].

question: What is the need of a Guru?

result.text:
In Bhakti-Yoga I set it down thus.
“The person from whose soul such impulse comes is called the Guru — the teacher; and the person to whose soul the impulse is conveyed is called the Shishya — the student. To convey such an impulse to any soul, in the first place, the soul from which it proceeds must possess the power of transmitting it, as it were, to another; and in the second place, the soul to which it is transmitted must be fit to receive it. The seed must be a living seed, and the field must be ready ploughed; and when both these conditions are fulfilled, a wonderful growth of genuine religion takes place. "The true preacher of religion has to be of wonderful capabilities, and clever shall his hearer be" — ; and when both of these are really wonderful and extraordinary, then will a splendid spiritual awakening result, and not otherwise. Such alone are the real teachers, and such alone are also the real students, the real aspirants. All others are only playing with spirituality. They have just a little curiosity awakened, just a little intellectual aspiration kindled in them, but are merely standing on the outward fringe of the horizon of religion.” [1]

question: What is the cause of evil in the world?

result.text:
I wrote of this in Jnana-Yoga, in the chapter Ch. 13: The Atman.
“With all dualistic theories the first difficulty is, how is it possible that under the rule of a just and merciful God, the repository of an infinite number of good qualities, there can be so many evils in this world? This question arose in all dualistic religions, but the Hindus never invented a Satan as an answer to it. The Hindus with one accord laid the blame on man, and it was easy for them to do so. Why? Because, as I have just now told you, they did not believe that souls were created out of nothing We see in this life that we can shape and form our future every one of us, every day, is trying to shape the morrow; today we fix the fate of the morrow; tomorrow we shall fix the fate of the day after, and so on. It is quite logical that this reasoning can be pushed backward too. If by our own deeds we shape our destiny in the future why not apply the same rule to the past? If, in an infinite chain, a certain number of links are alternately repeated then, if one of these groups of links be explained, we can explain the whole chain. So, in this infinite length of time, if we can cut off one portion and explain that portion and understand it, then, if it be true that nature is uniform, the same explanation must apply to the whole chain of time.” [1]

question: What is freedom?

result.text:
My hearers recorded me saying this in Freedom of the Self.
“Freedom is inseparably connected with immortality. To be free one must be above the laws of nature. Law exists so long as we are ignorant. When knowledge comes, then we find that law nothing but freedom in ourselves. The will can never be free, because it is the slave of cause and effect. But the "I" behind the will is free; and this is the Self. "I am free" — that is the basis on which to build and live. And freedom means immortality.” [1]

question: What is the ideal of Karma-Yoga?

result.text:
This is how I treated it in Karma-Yoga.
“The grandest idea in the religion of the Vedanta is that we may reach the same goal by different paths; and these paths I have generalised into four, viz those of work, love, psychology, and knowledge. But you must, at the same time, remember that these divisions are not very marked and quite exclusive of each other. Each blends into the other. But according to the type which prevails, we name the divisions. It is not that you can find men who have no other faculty than that of work, nor that you can find men who are no more than devoted worshippers only, nor that there are men who have no more than mere knowledge. These divisions are made in accordance with the type or the tendency that may be seen to prevail in a man. We have found that, in the end, all these four paths converge and become one. All religions and all methods of work and worship lead us to one and the same goal.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 1: Karma in Its Effect on Character]; [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 2: Each Is Great in His Own Place].
